{{No footnotes|date=October 2025}}

In mathematics, a '''bivariant theory''' was introduced by [[William Fulton (mathematician)|Fulton]] and [[Robert MacPherson (mathematician)|MacPherson]] {{harv|Fulton|MacPherson|1981}}, in order to put a [[Ring (mathematics)|ring structure]] on the [[Chow group]] of a [[singular variety]], the resulting ring called an '''[[operational Chow ring]]'''.

On technical levels, a bivariant theory is a mix of a [[homology (mathematics)|homology]] theory, specifically [[Borel–Moore homology|Borel-Moore homology]], and a [[cohomology]] theory.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Abe |first=Tomoyuki |date=2022 |title=Enhanced bivariant homology theory attached to six functor formalism |url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1112/topo.12249 |journal=Journal of Topology |language=en |volume=15 |issue=4 |pages=1675–1754 |doi=10.1112/topo.12249 |issn=1753-8424|url-access=subscription }}</ref> In general, a homology theory is a [[Covariance and contravariance (computer science)|covariant]] [[functor]] from the category of spaces to the category of [[abelian group]]s, while a cohomology theory is a [[contravariant functor]] from the category of (nice) spaces to the category of rings. A bivariant theory is a functor both covariant and contravariant; hence, the name “bivariant”.

== Definition ==
Unlike a homology theory or a cohomology theory, a bivariant class is defined for a map not a space.

Let <math>f : X \to Y</math> be a map. For such a map, we can consider the fiber square
:<math>
\begin{matrix}
X' & \to & Y' \\
\downarrow & & \downarrow \\
X & \to & Y
\end{matrix}
</math>
(for example, a blow-up.) Intuitively, the consideration of all the fiber squares like the above can be thought of as an approximation of the map <math>f</math>.

Now, a '''birational class''' of <math>f</math> is a family of group homomorphisms indexed by the fiber squares:
:<math>A_k Y' \to A_{k-p} X'</math>
satisfying the certain compatibility conditions.

== Operational Chow ring ==
{{expand section|date=October 2019}}<!-- this section is a draft -->
The basic question was whether there is a [[cycle map]]:
:<math>A^*(X) \to \operatorname{H}^*(X, \mathbb{Z}).</math>
If ''X'' is smooth, such a map exists since <math>A^*(X)</math> is the usual [[Chow ring]] of ''X''. {{harv|Totaro|2014}} has shown that rationally there is no such a map with good properties even if ''X'' is a [[linear variety (algebraic geometry)|linear variety]], roughly a variety admitting a cell decomposition. He also notes that Voevodsky's [[motivic cohomology ring]] is "probably more useful" than the operational Chow ring for a singular scheme (§ 8 of loc. cit.)
